knowledge_type_note: Motif (D), but recognition is heuristic: it depends on identifying a DUTY, which is a functional judgement rather than a geometric one.
definition_short: Forcing a defending piece away from the square, line, or duty it must hold.
definition_long:
The defender's piece is doing a job. Deflection forces it to stop — usually with a capture or a check it cannot decline — and the real target then falls.

Deflection and DECOY are constantly conflated; the useful distinction is one of direction. Deflection pushes a piece AWAY from a duty. A decoy lures a piece TOWARDS a bad square. Chess.com merges them into one theme; Chess Tempo and Chess Informant keep them separate (themes d and h). This record keeps them separate and cross-links them.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: An enemy piece is performing a defensive duty (guarding a square, a piece, or a line)
A forcing move exists that compels that piece to move or be captured
indicators_for: The deflecting move is a check or an offer the defender cannot decline
The duty is sole — no other unit covers it
indicators_against: A second defender covers the same duty
The defender can decline the offer and keep its post
Accepting costs the attacker more than the target is worth

typical_plans: Name the duty before naming the deflection: what is the piece holding, and what happens the moment it stops
Attack the defender with something it must take or must answer, rather than with something it can ignore
In the endgame, deflect the king rather than a piece — a king that must answer a check cannot also stop a pawn
typical_moves: A sacrifice on a square the defender is obliged to capture on
A check that forces the defending piece to interpose
A pawn push attacking the piece that guards a mating square
typical_piece_arrangements: A single piece defending two things at once — deflection and overloading are then the same move seen twice
A back rank guarded by exactly one rook
tactical_consequences: Deflection and decoy are the same sacrifice read from opposite ends: deflection removes a defender from a duty, decoy puts a victim on a square, and one move is very often both
The material given is usually irrelevant to the arithmetic — what matters is whether the duty can be abandoned

exceptions: A deflection fails if the deflected piece can answer the threat and keep its duty, which is the commonest miscalculation in the motif.
Deflecting a defender that has a second defender behind it achieves nothing.
If the opponent can decline, it is not a deflection — the whole idea rests on the reply being forced.
limitations: `themesOf()` refuses to claim deflection at all, and deliberately: every cheap test for it fires where it is not true, and a wrong label is worse than a missing one because the label is the thing the reader is learning to see.

by_level.beginner: This forces the defending piece to leave, and then the thing it was guarding is yours.
by_level.intermediate: Deflection: the defender is dragged off its job by a threat it cannot ignore.
by_level.advanced: Deflection (Informant theme d). Distinguish from decoy, which lures a piece onto a square rather than off a duty.
